There we could be sure of finding, invisibly present, all the pilgrims who had gone before us—not only Mîr Dâmâd, Mollâ Sadrâ, Mohsen Fayz, and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, but all those who, generation after generation, shaped Shiite thought and gave it its unique place in the religious history of humanity. (We shall return to this sanctuary later; see Book VII, Chapter II below.)
Yet Mollâ Sadrâ, in his turn, had to leave this landscape of mystical landmarks, whose center is the radiant dome of the sanctuary at Qomm.

Thus began the third period of his life. During his nine or eleven years at Kahak, he had reached the personal spiritual realization for which philosophy is the indispensable starting point, but without which philosophy, for him and for those who shared his outlook, would be a barren illusion.

However hard a personality of Mollâ Sadrâ's stature may try to keep his retreat secret, he can never quite succeed. He could not prevent students and disciples from seeking him out, and his reputation spread accordingly.

It is therefore not especially surprising to learn that Allâhwêrdî Khân—an Arabic-Persian name equivalent to our “God-given,” Adeodatus—who governed Fârs from 1003/1594–1595 until his death in 1021/1612, had a large madrasa, or college, built for our philosopher-shaykh in Shîrâz. He invited him to return to his native city and take charge of teaching at the new institution. This magnificent college still stands in Shîrâz (the Madrasa Khân), where one can visit the recently restored hall in which Mollâ Sadrâ gave his lectures.

I see no decisive reason to reject the explicit testimony of the historians who attribute this initiative to Governor Allâhwêrdî Khân. Nor is there reason to rule out the possibility that it was during the governor's lifetime, and therefore still under Shah 'Abbâs I (1587–1629), that Mollâ Sadrâ accepted the invitation to teach in Shîrâz and entered the third period of his life. When Allâhwêrdî Khân died, Mollâ Sadrâ was forty-one and in the fullness of his powers.

His teaching during these years in Shîrâz allows us to speak of a “School of Shîrâz” just as we have spoken of the “School of Ispahan.” Since Mollâ Sadrâ had been Mîr Dâmâd's disciple, this School of Shîrâz was also, in a sense, an offshoot of the School of Ispahan. Thomas Herbert, a seventeenth-century English traveler, recorded that “Shîrâz has a college where philosophy, astronomy, physics, chemistry and mathematics are taught, and it is the most famous college in Persia.”

We can readily picture Mollâ Sadrâ's life there. He lived wholly absorbed in teaching, writing his books—some of which, alas, remained unfinished—and looking after his students. Nothing defines him better than the high moral teaching he gave them and practiced throughout his own life. It can be summed up in four demands made of anyone who wishes to advance along the spiritual path: give up the possession of riches; give up worldly ambition and the pursuit of advancement; give up sectarian or unthinking conformity (taqlîd); and give up every form of the spirit of denial (ma'siyat).

These are the principles of an ethic entirely consistent with the strict distinction Mollâ Sadrâ drew between the “scholars of this world,” driven by worldly ambitions, and the “seekers of the other world”—those, as we might say today, whose inspiration remains directed toward the ultimate destiny of human life. Despite his enormous workload, Mollâ Sadrâ made the pilgrimage to Mecca seven times. He died at Basra on the return journey from his seventh pilgrimage and was buried there in 1050/1640.

The work through which this profound thinker, a spiritual man in the fullest sense—an intellectual who never betrayed his calling—continues to make his presence felt among us is immense. Almost all of it was published in Iran in lithographed editions during the last century; it comprises a little over forty titles.

Some books run to a hundred pages or so, while others are monumental works of several hundred folio pages. Together they address the whole range of Islamic philosophy. Some follow a plan shaped by Mollâ Sadrâ's own research; others are commentaries, but so expansive and original that they too must be considered works in their own right.

We have already noted that Mollâ Sadrâ wrote a commentary on the metaphysical portion of Avicenna's great Shifâ' (The Healing), as well as on Sohrawardî's major work, the Book of Oriental Theosophy (Hikmat al-Ishrâq). Later we shall offer extracts from this fundamental commentary, which brings into view two great moments in the Iranian tradition of Illumination (ishrâq).

In commenting on Kolaynî's Book of the Sources (al-Osûl mina'l-Kâfî), one of Shiism's foundational works preserving the teaching of the holy Imams, Mollâ Sadrâ was building a monumental Summa of Shiite philosophy, which he unfortunately did not live to complete. He also composed a Tafsîr, a commentary on extensive portions of the Qur'an. Its principal concern is to uncover the Qur'anic text's hidden, spiritual, or gnostic meaning.

Alongside the works of his predecessors and successors, it shows us how the spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an has been an essential source of philosophical meditation in Islam (see Books II and III above). This was especially bound to be true of Shiite Islam, for reasons we have already explained and will return to shortly.

The Summa in which Sadrâ Shîrâzî gathered the fruits of all his labors, investigations, and meditations is the celebrated work he called The Four Spiritual Journeys (Kitâb al-Asfâr al-arba'a al-'aqlîya). It is a monument of scholarship and thought, filling no fewer than a thousand folio pages in the old lithographed edition.

More than any other work, it stirred the devotion of disciples and commentators. Together they form an impressive succession, beginning with two of his most famous immediate disciples, both also his sons-in-law: Mohsen Fayz and 'Abdorrazzâq Lâhîjî. It continues from generation to generation down to our own time, taking in, during the last century, 'Abdollah Zonûzî and his son Mollâ 'Alî Zonûzî, Mollâ Hâdî Sabzavârî, and so many others.

Here, in outline, is more than three centuries of Iranian philosophy. The questions raised by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î and the Shaykhî school cannot be properly understood without a sound knowledge of Mollâ Sadrâ's work. That is why they have been so poorly understood by theologians unfamiliar with mystical gnosis ('irfân), though all the more eager to stamp about on ground that is slipping away beneath their feet.
In short, I maintain that no serious study of the philosophical situation of Shiism is possible without familiarity with Sadrâ Shîrâzî's thought and writings. That, ultimately, is what matters.

What deep intention animated him throughout his life? To answer, we must first resist the illusion that we have “explained” a philosopher or a philosophy merely by identifying and cataloguing its “sources” and “precursors.” Such an inventory only prepares the way for the essential task: to establish the breadth of the thinker's horizon, the angle from which he sees, and the underlying lines of thought that connect, for example, the metaphysics of being, the doctrine of the Imams, and the philosophy of Resurrection.

In the end, Mollâ Sadrâ can be explained only through Mollâ Sadrâ himself. We may collect all the sources, quotations, and allusions we please; none of them will ever produce a Mollâ Sadrâ unless there is already a Mollâ Sadrâ to bring them together into an order and a structure that only he could give them.

Earlier I spoke of “Shiism in its fullness,” because the mystical and theosophical implications of that fullness reveal the motive behind the philosopher's twofold spiritual struggle: first against himself, then against the dark forces of a hostile outer world.

Mollâ Sadrâ fought the first of these spiritual battles during his years of solitude at Kahak. Nothing less was at stake than his most personal destiny, the meaning of the course his life had taken, and the passage from the philosopher's theoretical speculation to the certainty that the gnostic—the 'ârif, the one who knows through direct experience—has lived and verified for himself. Unless these two forms of knowing are united, there is no complete philosopher, no philosopher in the truest sense. This has been the whole purpose of ishrâqî spirituality since Sohrawardî.
But for Sadrâ Shîrâzî, as for his predecessors and successors, the union finds its essential fulfillment within Shiite spirituality.
Let us examine the matter more closely.

The word ishrâq has enjoyed an extraordinary place in Iranian philosophy since Sohrawardî used it in the twelfth century to characterize the wisdom of ancient Persia that he sought to revive. There is little of substance to add here to our earlier discussion (Book II), but a reminder is never wasted when it helps us understand what follows.

Let us therefore bring together, in a few lines, the essentials we need to keep in mind in reading Mollâ Sadrâ. Ishrâq signifies the splendor of the rising dawn and the morning illumination that bathes all who are present to that dawn. It also signifies the source and origin of this light: the Orient, the place and hour of the rising sun.

Every part of this imagery must be carried over into the world beyond the senses. The “Orient” here means the world of Light and of beings of light; the dawning illumination rises from the Orient of the hierarchical Intelligences and falls upon human souls exiled in the western realm of darkness.

Let us recall as well that the wisdom arising from this Orient of the soul, and therefore called “Oriental” in keeping with this mystical geography, is neither philosophy nor theology in the ordinary modern sense of two separate disciplines whose relationship has to be worked out. This “Oriental” wisdom (hikmat mashriqîya or ishrâqîya) is divine wisdom, hikmat ilâhîya—the exact equivalent of the Greek theosophia.

It guides the seeker beyond the philosopher's abstract knowledge, which knows things through an intervening form or concept—a knowledge by representation ('ilm sûrî)—toward direct vision, toward the illumination of a presence that rises in the soul's own Orient. This other form of knowing is no longer called representational but knowledge by presence ('ilm hozûrî). It is “Oriental” knowledge because it illuminates, and it illuminates because it comes from the “Orient.”

As we have shown, this is the mystical meaning of “Orient” and “Oriental” in the phrase Oriental Theosophy (Hikmat al-Ishrâq), the divine wisdom which, for Sohrawardî, belonged to Zoroaster and the sages of ancient Persia. We have also seen that, in ordinary philosophical usage, the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of Illumination, are contrasted with the Mashshâ'ûn, the Peripatetics; in this sense the term corresponds to Platonists or Neoplatonists. These Neoplatonists of Islamic Persia have a long history, and they belong to the same spiritual family as Neoplatonists in every age and place.

“Oriental” knowledge, ishrâq, is the moment when the light of the soul's Orient—its origin before earthly existence—rises upon it. This was the very experience Mollâ Sadrâ lived through in the exalted solitude of Kahak.

He confides the experience to his reader in the prologue to his great work: “When I had persevered in that state of withdrawal, anonymity, and separation from the world for a long time,” he writes, “at last my inward striving set my soul ablaze; through repeated spiritual exercises my heart was kindled into towering flames.

“Then the lights of the Malakût, the angelic world, poured out upon my soul, while the secrets of the Jabarût, the world of pure cherubic Intelligences, were unfolded to it, and the mysteries of the divine Unity permeated it. I came to know divine secrets that I had never understood before; symbols and hidden meanings (romûz) were unveiled to me as no rational argument had ever been able to unveil them.

“Or rather: every metaphysical secret that I had previously known through rational demonstration I now perceived intuitively, in direct vision.” (Notice that the language describing this spiritual experience places it in complete harmony with those of Sohrawardî and Mîr Dâmâd. Unshakable certainty springs not from logical argument, but from immediate presence, experienced intuitively and sometimes in visions.) “Then,” Mollâ Sadrâ continues, “God inspired me to offer a sip of the drink I had tasted, to quench the thirst of those who seek [...].

“And so I have composed a book for pilgrims in search of spiritual perfection. In it I disclose a wisdom bestowed by God (hikmat rabbânîya) that can lead seekers toward the Majesty enveloped in Beauty and Rigor.”

That book is the great Summa Mollâ Sadrâ entitled The Four Spiritual Journeys. What did he mean by this title? He explains it himself at the end of the prologue. It draws on the traditional vocabulary of Islamic mystical gnosis. The first journey begins in the world of created beings and leads to God (mina'l-khalq ilâ'l-Haqq). Along the way it examines the composition of beings, the whole field of physics, matter and form, substance and accident. By its end, the pilgrim has risen to the suprasensible plane of divine realities.

The second journey then begins from God, in God, and through God (fî'l-Haqq bî'l-Haqq). Here the pilgrim remains on the metaphysical plane and is initiated into the Ilâhîyât, the Divinalia, the divine realities: questions concerning the divine Essence, Names, and Attributes.

The third journey follows a course of thought opposite to the first. It “descends” again from God to the world of created beings, but now “with God,” or “through God” (mina'l-Haqq ilâ'l-khalq bi'l-Haqq).

It follows the procession of beings from the Light of Lights and opens the way to knowledge of the hierarchical Intelligences and the multitude of suprasensible universes, whose levels rise above the physical world perceived by the senses. Here we encounter the whole of cosmogony and angelology.

Finally, the fourth journey takes place “with God,” or “through God,” within the created world itself (bi'l-Haqq fî'l-khalq). Above all, it initiates the pilgrim into knowledge of the soul, which means knowledge of oneself—the knowledge of the “Orient.” It also opens the way to esoteric tawhîd, the recognition that God alone truly is, and to the meaning of the saying: “Whoever knows his soul”—that is, whoever knows himself—“knows his Lord.”
Finally, it opens the perspectives of eschatology, of the great Return (Ma'âd): the boundless worlds awaiting the human being who has crossed the threshold of death.

These few lines can give only the faintest idea of the great Summa in which Sadrâ Shîrâzî erected a monument of Iranian Islamic thought. If we wished to characterize our shaykh in broad historical terms, we would have to list the distinguishing features of Shiite philosophy already encountered in the School of Ispahan.

In one sense, he is an Avicennian: Mollâ Sadrâ knew Avicenna's works extraordinarily well and wrote commentaries on them. At the same time, he is an ishrâqî Avicennian. That is to say, he has traveled the whole distance between Avicenna and Sohrawardî—a distance symbolized by the symbolic distance between the ending of Avicenna's story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân and the opening of Sohrawardî's Tale of the Western Exile.

Moreover, Sadrâ offers a highly personal interpretation of Sohrawardî's metaphysics of illumination. He is deeply steeped in the teachings of the great mystical theosopher Mohyiddîn Ibn 'Arabî (d. 1240), and, like Haydar Âmolî before him (see Book IV, Chapter I above), he invites us to investigate more deeply what might be called Ibn 'Arabî's implicit, or “crypto-,” Shiism.

Above all, however, Mollâ Sadrâ is a Shiite thinker, profoundly formed by the teachings of the holy Imams and committed to Islam as those teachings disclose it. These are only points of orientation. Neither the man nor his work can be “explained” as the sum or product of the influences we have just distinguished.

Prior to all of them stands what Ibn 'Arabî's vocabulary, which Sadrâ shares, calls his “eternal haecceity” ('ayn thâbita): his own individual archetype. This is what originally called the “materials” of his work together and fused them into the unique whole they became. It is therefore the first and final “explanation” of the structure of his entire work. The axis of that structure is the doctrine of the Shiite Imams, as we can see in his great commentary on Kolaynî's Book of the Sources—sources that are, in the fullest sense, the sources of “divine knowledge.”

Here Mollâ Sadrâ engages in his other spiritual struggle, this time against devout forms of agnosticism: blind literalism, an exclusively legal understanding of religion, and, in short, every attitude that for one reason or another rejects the Imams' teaching about the inner meaning of revelation, thereby rejecting the very essence of mystical gnosis, or 'irfân. Mollâ Sadrâ's stated intentions help us understand the philosophical situation of Shiism. They also reveal the enduring significance of his work and its continuing living power within Shiite thought.

How does the Shiite vision present itself to the 'orafâ—those who not only profess what is called 'irfân-e shî'î, Shiite gnosis, but regard Shiism itself, the doctrine of the Imams, as the very essence of Islam's inner spiritual knowledge, its esotericism: as Islam in its fullness and therefore as the true spiritual Islam? The answer emerges from the discussions already developed in this book (see Books I and IV above), in which Mollâ Sadrâ's commentary on Kolaynî's corpus, together with the writings of Haydar Âmolî, has served as our principal guide into the Imams' thought.

Yet, once again, because a recapitulation can be valuable, I think it useful to bring together the main steps that lead Mollâ Sadrâ to a thesis of decisive importance: that, within Islam, Shiism alone has been able to bring divine Revelation and philosophical intelligence into harmony, like the voices of a symphony.

For the 'orafâ, Shiite doctrine is founded on two inseparable poles: the sharî'at, the literal form of divine Revelation, and the haqîqat, that Revelation's spiritual, gnostic truth. These correspond to the outward, literal, visible aspect (zâhir) of divine Revelations and their inward, secret, esoteric reality (bâtin). Consequently, they correspond also to prophecy and the Imamate. Having stated the matter this way, we can trace the path that leads to it. For clarity, let us distinguish five stages.

Everyone agrees on why prophets are necessary. A prophet here is not someone who “predicts the future,” but an inspired, more-than-ordinary human being who delivers a divine message that humanity could never attain by its own powers. Prophets are therefore extraordinary human beings whom divine inspiration appoints as mediators between the unknowable Godhead and human ignorance or helplessness. There have been six great prophets entrusted with revealing a divine Law, a sharî'at, to humanity. Their names—Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Mohammad—mark the successive periods that together form the “cycle of prophecy” (dâ'irat al-nobowwat). The Prophet of Islam was the Seal of the Prophets (Khâtim al-anbiyâ'). After him, no further prophet will come to reveal a new divine Law.

The Shiite idea can be traced historically not only to the Prophet's immediate circle but also to what the Prophet himself said about the person closest to him, Imam 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib. This idea reveals the tragedy implicit in the closing of the prophetic message. Shiism asks a fundamental question: if humanity has always needed prophets in order to live through its destiny, what becomes of it now that the last prophet has come and there will never again be a prophet-messenger (rasûl)? A second, equally serious question follows. The Book revealed from heaven to a prophet is no ordinary book. Its meaning is not confined to its outward, literal wording, nor can it be exhausted through philology and dialectical reasoning. It is a Book with hidden depths. The secret meaning of a divine text, of a divine Word, cannot be reconstructed by syllogisms. It can only be handed down by “those who know” to those in whom this spiritual truth, in turn, becomes an immediate certainty, bringing about in them a new birth—their spiritual birth. Since the full reality of Qur'anic Revelation embraces both what is apparent and what is hidden, zâhir and bâtin, outward and inward meaning, there must remain after the Prophet a “Keeper of the Book” (Qayyim bi'l-Kitâb) who can initiate others into its complete meaning. This is the teaching of the Imams themselves; Mollâ Sadrâ is simply its interpreter.

This is why Shiite theology holds that the “cycle of prophecy” has been succeeded by the “cycle of walâyat,” the cycle of spiritual initiation and guidance. More precisely, what has ended is lawgiving prophecy (nobowwat al-tashrî'), the mission of a prophet who reveals a sharî'at. But under a new name, walâyat, another kind of prophecy continues: not the giving of a new Law, but a permanent prophecy concerned with inward and hidden realities, an esoteric prophetic message, or nobowwat bâtinîya. In Mollâ Sadrâ's vocabulary, the term follows from the very definition of walâyat as the “inward dimension of prophecy” (bâtin al-nobowwat). This permanent prophecy began at the dawn of earthly humanity and will continue until the appearance of the Imam who announces the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat).

The metaphysical foundation of this doctrine lies in the “Mohammadan Reality,” also called the “eternal Prophetic Reality” (Haqîqat mohammadîya). This reality has two “dimensions,” two “aspects,” and therefore requires two forms of manifestation. Its outward dimension appears in the lawgiving prophet; its inward dimension appears in the Imam. Together the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones” (tchahârdeh Ma'sûm)—the Prophet, his daughter Hazrat-e Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams—form the pleroma of light, the complete spiritual assembly of eternal prophecy. The twelve Imams share one and the same essence; their “persons of light” shone forth in pre-eternity. During their brief appearances on earth they were the “Keepers of the Book,” initiating disciples into its complete, inward meaning. (Their teachings, as we have said, fill several folio volumes.)

Just as the fullness of lawgiving prophecy had to be manifested on earth in the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets,” so the fullness of walâyat, the inward dimension of prophecy (bâtin al-nobowwat), had to be manifested in the “Seal of walâyat.” This Seal is the Mohammadan Imamate: in the First Imam, as the Seal of universal walâyat, common to every period of prophecy; and in the Twelfth Imam, as the Seal of Mohammadan walâyat. (This is the Shiite position that Haydar Âmolî defended so forcefully against Ibn 'Arabî; see Book II, Chapter I above.) Yet the Twelfth Imam, present both to the past and to the future, whose Manifestation—his return or parousia—will reveal the hidden meaning of every divine Revelation since the dawn of human life on earth, is at present invisible. We live in the time of his occultation (ghaybat), which will endure until human beings have made themselves capable of seeing him. In the figure of the Hidden Imam, Shiism has discerned the deepest mystery of human history, a mystery also foreshadowed in Zoroastrianism by the Saoshyant, in Buddhism by the Buddha to come, Maitreya, and in the Christianity of the spiritual reformers, from the thirteenth-century followers of Joachim of Fiore onward, by the expectation of the reign of the Holy Spirit.

Brief as this summary is, it is enough to remind us that Islamic philosophy and spirituality cannot be reduced to the three groups to which our histories have traditionally allotted their chapters on Islamic philosophy: the so-called Hellenizing philosophers (falâsifa), the Motakallimûn—the practitioners of Sunni Kalâm, or dialectical theology, representing the scholastic tradition of Islam—and, finally, the Sufis.

We already know that there is something more. It is precisely this further dimension that has helped us understand why philosophy, generally considered to have exhausted itself elsewhere in Islam after Averroes at the end of the twelfth century, underwent such a magnificent rebirth in the Shiite world of Iran, with the School of Ispahan.

When a researcher succeeds in entering the heart of Shiite thought, an entirely new horizon opens. Outside that horizon, the question of philosophy's place in Islam, and of its relation to Islamic dogma, has been posed on a false footing.

We have already seen why. Wherever it is held necessary to pass from what is apparent to what is hidden, from the outward to the inward meaning, facts themselves are transformed into symbols, and thought is called upon, again and again, to go beyond itself into the night of symbols.

A symbol is silence: it speaks, and it does not speak. It is not an allegory and can never be deciphered once and for all, as a celebrated saying of the Fifth Imam so aptly affirms. The first question, then, is whether one recognizes that divine Revelation has hidden meanings and, consequently, that there is an esoteric Islam into which the Imams initiated their followers—or whether one rejects all this outright in the name of a religion confined to the letter and the Law.

In the first case, philosophy will be at home, and it will take the form of a “prophetic philosophy.” In the second, there is no longer even any place to speak of philosophy. The tragedy endured by Mollâ Sadrâ, and by many others before and after him—including Haydar Âmolî, as we have seen, some three centuries earlier—was that their accusers called themselves Shiites too.

Yet the paradox is only apparent. In the eyes of the 'orafâ, the gnostics, some people may claim the name of Shiism while, by rejecting gnosis ('irfân), destroying what constitutes its very essence: the indissoluble union of zâhir and bâtin, outward and inward meaning.

An anguished echo of this tragedy runs through all Mollâ Sadrâ's writings. It was the tragedy that drove him into voluntary exile at Kahak, away from the persecution of zealots devoted to the letter and the Law. In the prologue to The Four Spiritual Journeys, for example, he denounces those willfully ignorant people whose minds cannot rise beyond the forms of material things, beyond the “dwellings of darkness and their dust.”

Hostile to a gnosis and philosophy they have never understood, they seek to banish all philosophy from the traditional religious sciences, even though this leaves them unable to understand the divine secrets expressed by the prophets in enigmas and symbols (romûz). These people declare that the gnostic philosophers have fallen victim to a divine ruse and have been led astray.

In his book The Three Sources, Mulla Sadra turns on one of these ignorant critics with magnificent force: “Have you not considered,” he asks, “that the person who has been led astray might be someone like you? If all knowledge is as you understand it, if it must be received word for word from tradition and from the shaykhs, why does God, in several verses of the Quran, condemn those who base their beliefs on just such conformity and put their trust in it? When the Commander of the Faithful, the First Imam, declares, ‘If I wished, I could produce a commentary on the opening surah of the Quran alone that would weigh as much as seventy camel-loads,’ did he acquire such knowledge from a human teacher, through ordinary instruction?”

Mulla Sadra then appeals to the very texts Haydar Amoli had invoked three centuries before him. To begin with, those who seek inner knowledge have the decisive authority of the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-Abidin (d. 95/714), who declares in one of his poems: “I hide the jewels of my Knowledge, for fear that an ignorant man, seeing the truth, might crush us. ... Lord, if I disclosed a single pearl of my gnosis, they would say to me: ‘So you are an idolater!’ And some Muslims would consider it lawful to shed my blood!

“What is most beautiful in what is offered to them, they find abhorrent.” What, Mulla Sadra asks, is this knowledge of which the Imam speaks so movingly—this sublime knowledge, beyond ordinary understanding, which makes someone appear impious, even idolatrous, in the eyes of the Muslim majority? His answer is straightforward. He finds it in a declaration by Abdallah ibn Abbas, one of the Prophet’s best-known Companions, who once exclaimed before a gathering near Mecca: “If I revealed to you how I heard the Prophet himself interpret the verse concerning the creation of the seven heavens and the seven earths (65:12), you would stone me.”

Thus anyone admitted, by divine grace, to the ultimate secret of the prophetic message risks being stoned by an enraged crowd of the ignorant. Must we look any further for the reasons behind the tragedy? Is there any other explanation for why the Imams of Shiism were surrounded by no more than a handful of knights of the faith?

Mulla Sadra can therefore readily show that the knowledge which so frightens ordinary people and the doctors of religious law is neither dialectics nor philology, medicine nor astronomy, geometry nor physics. None of what the interpreters concerned only with the Quran’s outward meaning—Zamakhshari and others like him, for example—offer is the Quran’s true knowledge, the true inner understanding of divine Revelation.

All of it belongs to philology, grammar, and dialectics; it never penetrates beyond the husk, the outer covering. The Quran’s true knowledge is something altogether different. And it is precisely this genuine understanding of the Quran, grounded in the Imams’ esoteric teaching, that assigns the philosopher the task of prophetic philosophy.

To make clear the “straight path” (sirat mustaqim)—or, to use a traditional expression going back to Philo, the “royal road”—which steers equally clear of the literalism of a religion reduced to law and of a rationalism that simply denies, Sadra explains the role of philosophical reflection in the prologue to his commentary on Book III of Kolayni’s great work, the Kitab al-Hujja, a treatise on the Imam and the Imamate.

Quranic Revelation is the light that makes sight possible; but it can do so only when the teaching of the Imams lifts the veil of literal appearances that covers it. Philosophical reflection is the eye that sees and contemplates that light. For vision to occur there must be light, but there must also be eyes that look. Remove the light and the eyes will see nothing.

Yet stubbornly close the eyes—as the literalists and doctors of the Law do—and nothing will be seen either. In both cases darkness triumphs; nor is the condition of someone who opens only one eye, and so sees with the vision of a one-eyed man, any better. Bring philosophical understanding and divine Revelation together, however, and there is “light upon light,” as the Verse of Light says (Quran 24:35).

Indeed, as we know, the successive parts of that Quranic verse refer, in their esoteric meaning, to the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. This is why Mulla Sadra solemnly proclaims his thesis: in Islam, the Shiite school alone has achieved this harmony, this symphony of divine Revelation and philosophical understanding. It has done so because the Shiites draw their knowledge and wisdom from the “Niche of Lights” of prophecy and walayat—the spiritual authority and guidance of the Imams. In other words, the philosophy of Shiism is, in its very essence, “prophetic philosophy.”

We should not be too quick to assimilate this situation to others familiar to us. What had to be overcome here was not a conflict between contingent historical truths and necessary truths of reason, nor the question of how truth can be historical and how history can be truth. That has been the whole problem of faith and knowledge confronted by Christian philosophy, from Origen through Leibniz to Hegel.

Nor was it a conflict between dogmatic truths defined by the authority of a Church’s teaching office and philosophical truths discovered through personal effort. No: the light of the holy Book, unveiled by the Imam as a personal guide, shines directly, without intermediary, upon the believer’s inner vision. Philosophy and theology do not confront one another as two already established authorities, one belonging to the individual and the other to an institutional teaching office. Their separation is a phenomenon peculiar to the West, with roots in medieval scholasticism.

By contrast, we must always bear in mind that, for our “Eastern” thinkers, the being of the Pleroma, the fullness of the heavenly world—the Angel whom philosophers call the Active Intellect ('aql fa''al, the Greek nous poietikos), is identified with the Holy Spirit who communicates divine Revelation to the prophets. This heavenly Intellect is also the source of our knowledge.

We have insisted on this point before: identifying the Angel of Knowledge with the Angel of Revelation does not mean reducing Spirit to reason. It means that the calling of the prophet and that of the philosopher bear a common imprint. This is precisely what allows philosophy, at its highest point, to become “prophetic philosophy.”

We are therefore very far from the doctrine of “double truth” that emerged in Western Averroism. Here, in “Eastern” philosophy, two lights come together and interpenetrate, giving rise to hikmat ilahiya: divine wisdom, or theosophy, which the Imams themselves were the first to call ma'rifat qalbiya, the knowledge of the heart. For Mulla Sadra, this is Shiism—Shiism in its fullness.

We can now see even more clearly why a thinker for whom the inner, gnostic faith of Shiism is fundamental should also be, quite naturally, an Ishraqi, a philosopher of illumination. What, after all, did Suhrawardi teach? That mystical experience without prior philosophical formation runs a serious risk of going astray. Conversely, as we recalled above, a philosophy that neither seeks nor leads to personal spiritual realization is sheer vanity. The whole design of The Book of Eastern Theosophy answers to this demand.

In a densely argued passage of his commentary on Kolayni, Mulla Sadra in turn places the spirituality of the Ishraqiyun, the philosophers of illumination, in an intermediate position—a barzakh, a place of meeting between two ways. It joins the method of the Sufis, whose chief aim is inner purification, with the method of the philosophers, who seek pure knowledge. We have already referred twice to this passage, so decisive does it seem to us for understanding the spirituality of Iranian Islam.

After commenting on the Imams’ theory of knowledge and distinguishing the various degrees of inspiration (ilham), Mulla Sadra pauses in this passage to discuss the Sufis’ spiritual method at some length. He observes: “As for reflective thinkers, and those who know how to take the measure of things (dhawu'l-i'tibar), they certainly do not deny the existence of this method or the possibility that it may reach its goal in exceptional cases. Such, indeed, was the case with most of the spiritual states (ahwal) experienced by the prophets and the awliya, the friends of God.

“Outside such cases, however, they consider the method hazardous; they judge its fruits slow to ripen and doubt that all the conditions it requires will ever be met. ...” His final conclusion is this: “The best course is for the pilgrim journeying toward God (al-salik ila'llah) to bring the two methods together.

“Let his inner discipline and purification (tasfiya) never be without philosophical reflection (tafakkur); and, conversely, let his philosophical reflection never be without an effort toward spiritual purification. Better still, let his spiritual method itself be a barzakh, an intermediate way joining the two paths (bayna'l-tariqayn). Such is the path followed by the Hukama' Ishraqiyun, the Eastern theosophers.” This is exactly the doctrine Suhrawardi professes in the prologue to his great book.

This position also explains why Mulla Sadra could sometimes speak harshly of certain Sufis: those who make a show of despising intellectual effort and whose contempt for philosophy leaves them just as blind as their opposites, the little-minded defenders of a religion reduced to law.

In fact, Sadra Shirazi belongs, along with many others, to a type of Shiite spiritual seeker who speaks the technical language of Sufism without belonging to any organized tariqa, or Sufi order. For Shiite 'irfan—the inner knowledge of Shiism—is already itself the tariqa, the spiritual path; and the bond of personal devotion to the holy Imams is already the beginning of initiation.
From here we can begin to see how Mulla Sadra’s major doctrines form a coherent whole, though we shall confine ourselves to two fundamental aspects.
First, his metaphysics of being culminates in a metaphysics of Presence; as this rises into a metaphysics of “witnessing,” it reaches the summit of prophetic philosophy.

Second, from that very summit we can trace a continuous line toward a metaphysics of active Imagination and the imaginal world, culminating in a metaphysics of Resurrection. Mulla Sadra himself will lay out this continuous line when he summarizes his whole doctrine in eight theses (below, § 4). Here we shall briefly recall how his metaphysics of being becomes a metaphysics of Presence.

We shall then draw out the principal features of his metaphysics of Resurrection from the final portion of his extensive commentary on Suhrawardi’s Book of Eastern Theosophy. Since we have just heard him explicitly identify himself with the spiritual method of the Ishraqiyun, we will thus have brought together these two moments of “Eastern theosophy” as defining moments in Iranian philosophy and spirituality.

Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics of being is “revolutionary” in that it overturns the venerable metaphysics of essences taught by Farabi, Avicenna, Suhrawardi, and many other “essentialists.” In their account of reality, an essence or quiddity (mahiyya)—what a thing is—remains immutably what it is. The word is, in saying so, does not imply actual existence. Existence was held to be merely a way of considering an essence, adding nothing to it because it did not constitute what that essence was.

Mulla Sadra reverses this perspective. In his commentary on Suhrawardi, this reversal will allow him to give the metaphysics of Ishraq, or illumination, an “existential” interpretation. Readers will find far more technical detail than we can offer here in our translation of and commentary on the Book of Metaphysical Penetrations (Kitab al-Masha'ir).

In particular, we showed there how illuminating it is to compare the vocabulary of being in Latin and Greek with its vocabulary in Arabic and Persian. Such comparisons will provide a foundation for the comparative study of being that still awaits us. For the first ways in which different traditions understand being reveal affinities or deep differences between philosophical systems and, through them, between cultures—even between different regions of a single culture.

In Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics of being, no essence precedes its own act of existing. An essence is by being what it is; the intensity of its act of being what it is determines the degree to which it exists. This act of being can take place at every level of the scale of existence, from mental existence (wujud dhihni) through all the levels of existence beyond the mind: sensible, imaginal, and intelligible.

Since it is the act of being that determines an essence, the same essence, far from being immutable, can undergo degrees of intensification or weakening according to its acts of being, along a scale that is practically without limit. Motion is thereby introduced into the very category of substance. This gives rise to Mulla Sadra’s distinctive doctrine of “intrasubstantial motion” (harakat jawhariyya).

No longer do we have, as we did with his philosophical predecessors, a realm of unchanging essences. In his thought we can speak of a mobility, a restless striving within being, extending from one end of the scale of beings to the other. An essence is thus capable of passing through a cycle of metamorphoses, each stage corresponding to another level of the universe.
Consider, for example, the idea of a body. To understand its essence, we must not confine its act of being to the physical world as perceived by the senses.

We must follow it from the simple Element—the word denoting, in traditional physics, essentially a qualitative state—through successive metamorphoses: from mineral to plant, from plant to animal, and then to the state of a living, speaking body capable of understanding spiritual realities. There is a material body, but there is also a psychic body and a spiritual body (caro spiritualis).

We shall see later that each of these last two is the “temple,” the dwelling place, of a future rebirth and resurrection. During our present earthly life, we determine whether we shall be capable of such a resurrection or whether, defeated, we shall fall below what we could have become.
